articles.title: Após derrota colossal, Partido Republicano tenta encontrar caminho para se recuperar do fracasso nas urnas | G1
articles.standfirst: O partido sabe que está diante de um momento decisivo. É preciso encontrar as lideranças que vão substituir Donald Trump depois de uma década.
articles.summary: O partido sabe que está diante de um momento decisivo. É preciso encontrar as lideranças que vão substituir Donald Trump depois de uma década.
articles.body:
Quarenta e oito horas depois da derrota colossal, o Partido Republicano tenta encontrar um caminho para se recuperar do fracasso nas urnas.

Passado o susto, o partido do presidente Donald Trump agora se deita no divã. Ron DeSantis, governador em fim de mandato na Flórida, definiu: a onda azul na verdade foi um meteoro e a eleição quase beira a extinção para os republicanos em muitas regiões do país.

Os resultados desse meteoro já começam a aparecer. Na Câmara, o presidente da Casa, Mike Johnson, já anunciou que em 2027 não quer o cargo de líder da minoria. E, nos bastidores, tem crescido o número de republicanos que culpam o secretário de Guerra, Pete Hegseth, por incentivar Trump a atacar o Irã . Segundo a imprensa americana, o Congresso pode votar um pedido de impeachment contra Hegseth já na semana que vem, com apoio de parlamentares do próprio partido.

O vice J.D. Vance também não perdeu tempo. Horas depois do resultado, publicou um texto em que procura se distanciar das políticas da Casa Branca e listou quatro reivindicações dos americanos: acabar com a guerra, focar no custo de vida e na inflação, colocar o país em primeiro lugar e mudar as relações dos Estados Unidos com Israel. Questionado sobre as críticas do próprio vice, Trump reconheceu que a guerra contra o Irã atrapalhou, mas disse que faria tudo de novo para evitar que o regime dos aiatolás desenvolva uma arma nuclear.

Após derrota colossal, Partido Republicano tenta encontrar caminho para se recuperar do fracasso nas urnas — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Julian Zelizer, historiador e professor de Políticas Públicas da Universidade Princeton, afirma que um dos maiores obstáculos para a criação de um novo caminho pode ser o próprio Donald Trump:

"O problema que os republicanos enfrentam é que Trump ainda conta com muito apoio dentro do partido. Eles estão atrelados a um líder que os prejudica e que não se importa com eles. É uma posição muito difícil”.

O partido sabe que está diante de um momento decisivo. É preciso encontrar as lideranças que vão substituir Donald Trump depois de uma década , e esse futuro precisa incluir eleitores do movimento Maga, "Faça a América Grande de Novo", que engloba o trumpismo mais radical, e dos republicanos tradicionais, mais ao centro. Esse futuro, segundo Zelizer, deve vir de lideranças locais:

“Se houver esse movimento, terá que ser dos governadores, de pessoas que estejam verdadeiramente desconectadas do partido em nível nacional. É para onde o partido terá que olhar”.

articles.title: Vitória dos democratas consagra nomes que terão um peso importante nos próximos anos | G1
articles.standfirst: O Partido Democrata, que passou por uma crise com a derrota para Trump nas eleições presidenciais em 2024, agora vive uma onda de esperança. Mas ainda dividido sobre qual caminho seguir.
articles.summary: O Partido Democrata, que passou por uma crise com a derrota para Trump nas eleições presidenciais em 2024, agora vive uma onda de esperança. Mas ainda dividido sobre qual caminho seguir.
articles.body:
O resultado contundente nas eleições para o Congresso americano, na terça-feira (3), foi uma vitória coletiva dentro do Partido Democrata, de oposição, e consagrou nomes que terão um peso importante nos próximos anos.

Jon Ossoff tem 39 anos. Repare bem na roupa e na forma como ele discursa para os eleitores. Você se lembra de alguém? O ex-presidente Barack Obama é uma referência para o senador reeleito com folga pela Geórgia, um estado onde Donald Trump venceu na última eleição presidencial. O resultado desta semana fortaleceu Jon Ossoff como um dos políticos democratas que mais se destacaram nos últimos dois anos.

O partido, que passou por uma crise com a derrota para Trump nas eleições presidenciais em 2024, agora vive uma onda de esperança. Mas ainda dividido sobre qual caminho seguir. A eleição foi praticamente um referendo sobre o presidente Donald Trump. E não dá para dizer que uma corrente específica foi a grande responsável pela vitória maiúscula de meio de mandato. As urnas consolidaram nomes dentro de um arco político que vai da ala mais à esquerda ao centro.

Vitória dos democratas consagra nomes que terão um peso importante nos próximos anos — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Abdul El-Sayed, eleito senador pelo Michigan, representa a primeira corrente e tem a companhia da deputada Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, de Nova York. Já candidatos mais alinhados ao centro foram fundamentais para resultados expressivos em regiões com tradição no Partido Republicano. Como o pastor presbiteriano James Talarico, eleito pelo Texas.

Para reconquistar os votos de eleitores rurais, latinos, negros e jovens, os candidatos democratas em todo o país fizeram campanha principalmente pela redução do custo de vida. Segundo o prefeito de Nova York, Zohran Mamdani, um voto de confiança que o partido não pode desperdiçar nos próximos dois anos, mirando conquistar novamente a Casa Branca.

Zohran Mamdani não nasceu nos Estados Unidos , mas sim em Uganda, na África. Por isso, ele não pode ser presidente do país. Mesmo assim, o prefeito de Nova York tem tido papel no sucesso do Partido Democrata. Para ele, chegou a hora de o partido atender às demandas do eleitor.

O tsunami azul - cor do Partido Democrata - tomou conta dos Estados Unidos e não tem apenas um dono. Levou a crise embora e trouxe novas opções para o futuro.

articles.title: Tereza Cristina diz que vai discutir disputa pelo Senado com Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Senadora afirmou que pretende apresentar ao ex-presidente sua visão sobre a eleição para o comando da Casa; defesa de Bolsonaro pediu autorização ao STF para que ele receba Tereza e Rogério Marinho.
articles.summary: Senadora afirmou que pretende apresentar ao ex-presidente sua visão sobre a eleição para o comando da Casa; defesa de Bolsonaro pediu autorização ao STF para que ele receba Tereza.
articles.body:
Senadora Tereza Cristina (PP-MS) em pronunciamento à bancada — Foto: Carlos Moura/Agência Senado

A senadora Tereza Cristina (PP-MS) afirmou nesta quinta-feira (5) que pretende discutir com o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL) a disputa pela presidência do Senado durante uma eventual visita a ele, que cumpre prisão domiciliar em Brasília.

Questionada se abriria mão de sua candidatura caso Bolsonaro pedisse apoio a Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), a parlamentar evitou se comprometer e afirmou não saber se o ex-presidente faria esse pedido. A declaração foi dada durante um jantar de gala promovido pela Câmara de Comércio França-Brasil, no hotel Rosewood, em São Paulo. Tereza foi homenageada com o Prêmio Personalidade do Ano 2026.

Questionada sobre o objetivo da visita, a senadora afirmou que já havia solicitado outras vezes a oportunidade de encontrar Bolsonaro e que pretende apresentar ao ex-presidente sua avaliação sobre a disputa pelo comando do Senado.

“Olha, eu sou amiga do presidente Bolsonaro, fui ministra dele. Eu já tinha pedido algumas vezes para visitá-lo e, agora, ele pedindo e acatando aquele meu pedido anterior, eu acho ótimo. Mas vamos poder conversar, explicar para ele o que está acontecendo, enfim, a minha visão do que é hoje a nossa missão nessa eleição do Senado, a minha e de Rogério Marinho”, afirmou.

Ao ser questionada se desistiria da candidatura caso Bolsonaro pedisse que a oposição se unificasse em torno de Marinho, Tereza evitou antecipar uma decisão.

“Eu não sei se o presidente me pediria isso, mas é claro que eu e o Rogério Marinho temos conversado desde o início. Ele tem dito isso, eu tenho repetido, mas parece que as pessoas não conseguem entender. Nós temos uma estratégia. A estratégia do nosso campo é ganhar o Senado”, disse.

A senadora também afirmou que não pretende enfrentar Marinho diretamente na eleição e que os dois deverão decidir, mais perto da votação, quem representará a oposição.

“Ele disse, no lançamento da candidatura dele: ‘Eu não enfrentarei a Tereza’. E eu vou dizer aqui: eu não enfrentarei o Rogério Marinho. Um de nós dois, lá na frente, nós temos que sentar com maturidade, responsabilidade que nós temos pelas pautas em que acreditamos, para não deixar o Senado apequenado, para que a gente possa pensar mais no Brasil”, declarou.

Tereza Cristina é um dos nomes que disputam a presidência do Senado para o próximo biênio, a partir de fevereiro de 2027. A senadora busca apoio para enfrentar o atual presidente da Casa, Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil-AP), que tenta a reeleição.

A disputa também envolve Rogério Marinho, que teve sua candidatura oficializada pelo PL nesta quarta-feira (4). Líder da oposição no Senado, Marinho tenta reunir o apoio dos partidos de direita para enfrentar Alcolumbre, que conta com o respaldo do governo Lula.

Tereza e Marinho discutem a possibilidade de unificar as candidaturas da oposição, mas ainda não chegaram a um acordo sobre quem abriria mão da disputa. A senadora do PP mantém articulações com parlamentares de diferentes partidos e afirma que a decisão será tomada mais perto da eleição.

A votação está marcada para 1º de fevereiro de 2027, quando os 81 senadores escolherão, por voto secreto, o presidente da Casa. Para vencer, um candidato precisa conquistar pelo menos 41 votos.

Em meio às articulações, a defesa do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL) pediu ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), autorização para que ele receba Tereza Cristina e Rogério Marinho em sua residência, onde cumpre prisão domiciliar. O pedido foi apresentado em um momento em que os dois senadores disputam o apoio da direita para a eleição interna do Senado.

articles.title: Hegseth faces bipartisan impeachment threat after Iran war gets blame for GOP midterm slaughter
articles.summary: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth faces a bipartisan impeachment threat as House Republicans say a privileged resolution could pass when Congress returns.
articles.body:
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is facing a bipartisan impeachment threat when Congress returns next week as Republicans seethe over their devastating losses in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Bipartisan frustration over the war in Iran , quietly simmering for months, is now openly erupting after Democrats stunned the country with historic victories in the House and Senate. That anger could all now hit Hegseth, with several House Republicans telling Fox News Digital that they believe a resolution to impeach him could pass as early as next week.

"He's screwed," one House GOP lawmaker told Fox News Digital.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a longtime critic of foreign intervention by the U.S., told Fox News Digital he intends to force a vote on impeaching Hegseth when Congress returns if the Pentagon chief does not resign first.

He'll do so by filing a privileged resolution, a mechanism aimed at getting a vote on legislation despite opposition from the majority party's leaders. Once a privileged resolution is filed, lawmakers have two legislative days to hold a vote.

But the procedure notably carries two steps. Before a vote on the measure itself, leaders can call up a vote to "table" the bill or refer it to the relevant committee, which in both instances effectively kills it.

That procedural vote is normally where most privileged resolutions die. But in this case, several House Republicans told Fox News Digital they believe the impeachment resolution could ultimately be successful.

"If he introduces it, it'll pass," a second House Republican told Fox News Digital. Two more said they expected the same.

One GOP lawmaker said attendance could be a key factor in impeaching Hegseth. It's highly possible that many Republicans who lost re-election simply do not return for the final two months of the year, that person said. And with just a razor-thin majority, only a handful of absences would be enough for Hegseth to get impeached if all Democrats stuck together.

The Fox News Decision Desk projected Democrats taking the House shortly before midnight on Tuesday. Projections showed that the war in Iran, along with tariff policies, were key drivers in voters turning their backs on the GOP.

And while President Donald Trump told reporters he believes Hegseth is doing "a good job," people in his circle appear to have their knives out.

"Hegseth is on the chopping block," a former White House official told Fox News Digital.

A current White House official said, "[Tuesday] would have looked very different without the Iran war. I believe you'll ultimately see [Trump] hold Pete Hegseth accountable and that will play out in the lame duck."

But the White House criticized the potential impeachment push on Thursday.

"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

And another White House official said, "If crazed Democrats want to abuse their power and politicize their process of investigations, subpoenas, and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell on Wednesday dismissed rumors that Trump could get rid of Hegseth himself.

"Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists. The Department of War has followed the law and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America," he told Fox News Digital.

It's also worth noting that the majority of House Republicans will still oppose impeaching Hegseth — and many are still skeptical.

"I really doubt [it]," another House Republican told Fox News Digital. "Depends on if anyone wants to flip off the president walking out the door."

There is likely to be healthy support on the other side of the aisle for such a push as well.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker, has consistently criticized Hegseth. He posted on X Thursday morning, "Why is Pete Hegseth still around?"

Even more moderate Democrats have signaled their support, given the administration did not seek the consent of Congress at any point during the ordeal.

"I've said a long, long time ago that he's not qualified for the job, and he should be removed, and I think we're going to pursue that," Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., who is expected to take over leadership of the House Armed Services Committee next year, told CNN's "This Morning" last month.

If Hegseth were impeached, he would not be removed before a trial in the U.S. Senate.

Fox News Digital reached out to the committee's Republican majority and the Pentagon for comment.
authors: Elizabeth Elkind, Ashley J. DiMella, Morgan Phillips

articles.title: House Democrats Surpass 250 Seats After Midterms
articles.summary: House Democrats Surpass 250 Seats After Midterms
articles.body:
Democrats continued to pick up seats in the House of Representatives on Thursday, reaching their highest total since 2009.

The Associated Press projects Democrats will win 252 seats, with 19 races still uncalled. Democrats have already flipped 38 seats.

Rep. Mike Turner, R-Ohio, a former chair of the House Intelligence Committee, was defeated by Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, the AP projected. Turner was first elected in 2002.

Rep. Richard Hudson, R-N.C., chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, was defeated by Richard Ojeda, the AP projected. Hudson conceded his race Wednesday.

Republican Reps. Juan Ciscomani of Arizona and Jeff Crank of Colorado were also defeated.

The GOP managed to flip only one seat in a district unaffected by mid-decade redistricting: Maine's 2nd Congressional District.

Among the uncalled House races is New York's 17th Congressional District, where Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., has already conceded to Democrat Cait Conley.

Republicans also fell short of their redistricting goals. The GOP targeted 15 Democratic-held districts, while Democrats countered with new maps targeting six Republican-held seats, potentially giving the GOP a net nine-seat advantage.

Instead, Democrats retained at least 11 of the 15 targeted seats, while Republicans flipped two, with two races unresolved as of Thursday.

In North Carolina, Democrats could win 10 of the state's 14 House seats, despite redistricting that favored Republicans in 11 districts.

Sen. Ted Cruz, the only statewide Republican official left in Texas after the midterms, called the GOP's losses a "Watergate-level repudiation," attributing the defeats to rising living costs and criticizing President Donald Trump's tariffs and the war with Iran.

articles.title: Trump to nominate Texas Supreme Court justice who lost election to federal bench
articles.summary: Nov 5 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump is moving to nominate a Republican member of the Texas Supreme Court who voters ousted from office ‌in Tuesday's...
articles.body:
Nov 5 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump is moving to nominate a Republican member of the Texas Supreme Court who voters ousted from office ‌in Tuesday's election to become a life-tenured federal judge, according to US Senate ‌records made public on Thursday.

Trump has not announced any such nomination. But the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee has ​received paperwork to begin considering outgoing Texas Supreme Court Justice James Sullivan to serve as a federal judge in Austin.

His nomination to a seat on the US District Court for the Western District of Texas will be taken up by the Senate during the lame-duck session in ‌the final weeks before Democrats take ⁠control of the chamber in January.

The White House and Sullivan did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Republicans are pushing to confirm nearly ⁠two dozen pending judicial nominees and add to 56 confirmed so far during Trump's second term before they hand over control of the Senate to Democrats.

Trump made 234 judicial appointments in his first ​term, ​including three Supreme Court justices, helping shift the ​federal judiciary's ideological balance to the ‌right.

Over Democrats' objections, Republican US Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa, the committee's outgoing chair, scheduled judicial nomination hearings in consecutive weeks starting November 10, departing from the panel's typical practice of holding them every other week.

Sullivan, 45, was appointed to the Texas Supreme Court in January 2025 to fill a vacancy on the state's top court by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ‌who lost his bid for reelection on Tuesday ​to Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Democrats in the election won all ​four seats up for a vote on ​the state's nine-member high court, shrinking the Republican majority on the ‌Texas Supreme Court to 5-4.

Sullivan's campaign website ​touted him as "bold," "relentless," and "conservative." ​He lost Tuesday's election to Chari Kelly, a Democrat, and in a Senate questionnaire submitted to the Senate Judiciary Committee, Sullivan noted his candidacy to retain his seat ​had been "unsuccessful."

Such questionnaires are submitted ‌to the committee by the US Department of Justice, and the Trump administration ​at times has submitted them before nominations have been officially announced.

(Reporting by ​Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Bill Berkrot)

articles.title: Hegseth in ‘trouble’ as Trump faces music on Iran war, midterms
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s future leading the Pentagon looks increasingly uncertain as his critics within the administration blame him for helping push...
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's future leading the Pentagon looks increasingly uncertain as his critics within the administration blame him for helping push President Trump into a war that contributed to massive midterm losses Tuesday.

Two sources familiar with the discussion said the president is asking allies about Hegseth's standing. One of those sources said the Defense chief is in "a lot of trouble," while the other said it wasn't clear how much his position was in jeopardy. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.

At the same time, the administration is reviewing plans to resume military operations against Iran, one of the two sources said.

Trump has stood by Hegseth in public and told reporters Thursday his mind wasn't made up on the future of the war.

"I would rather not destroy the rest of the country, if possible, but maybe I will have to," Trump told reporters Thursday at the White House. "You will know soon enough."

A senior Pentagon official told The Hill on Thursday that the idea of Hegseth being replaced is not "practical," pointing to the potential difficulty of finding a replacement who could be confirmed by the Senate during the lame-duck — and before Democrats take control of the upper chamber.

"He is not terribly worried about being replaced," the senior Pentagon official said.

The Defense secretary's standing in Congress has been on a downturn among both Democrats and Republicans, who have demanded more transparency from the Pentagon regarding the Iran war and defense spending plans.

A Republican congressional official said Hegseth's position had become "completely untenable" from a Capitol Hill standpoint.

"Keeping him in would require the White House to spend all of their political capital defending him from impeachment proceedings and drag the president into endless news cycles about the war, firing generals, Signalgate and more," this official told The Hill on Thursday.

Hegseth and allied social media accounts made a concerted effort to push back Thursday.

In a video recorded in front of the Pentagon, Hegseth slammed Rep. Thomas Massie's (R-Ky.) impeachment salvo and pushed once again for Congress to greenlight the $350 billion defense reconciliation package.

"This is not about me, but of course the other side. In case you've noticed, they're obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman , along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in the video posted Thursday.

"You see, their policies don't work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents," he said. "It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."

The Pentagon press team started making social media posts in support of the Defense secretary Thursday, writing, "Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic."

The Pentagon did not respond to The Hill's request for comment.

The White House posted an 80-second video to the social platform X touting Hegseth's tenure at the Pentagon.

"We are not defenders anymore. We are warriors," the Pentagon chief said in that video.

The speculation surrounding Hegseth's future follows Vice President Vance's move to blame the GOP's midterm defeats on the Iran war, of which he's been a vocal opponent within the administration.

"When you have the sitting VP say Iran is a mistake, the support for the conflict and Hegseth by extension is going to evaporate," one defense-world source said Thursday.

But a senior administration official said anyone "looking to point fingers should start looking for another scapegoat," as the Pentagon and the White House have made their positions on Hegseth "crystal clear."

"They are coming out swinging in support of Hegseth, and that should tell you everything you need to know," the official said.

"Suggesting he's looking for an exit or preparing to step aside is delusional thinking and misreading the situation. He's not going anywhere," the official added. "He's going to remain focused on his mission, he won't be distracted by the noise and he's not going to let the pressure dictate his future."

Inside the Pentagon, questions are swirling about how long Hegseth lasts even if he is not impeached, The Hill has reported.

Those who have broken with Hegseth, including a former Army National Guard major, argued the former Fox News co-host shouldn't have overseen the Pentagon in the first place.

"For almost two years now, we've had a cross between a court jester and a personal trainer running the Pentagon, and it's done real damage to the President and to Republicans. If Hegseth were truly loyal to President Trump, he would have stepped aside long ago — or better yet, never taken a job he wasn't qualified for," said John Ullyot, former Pentagon spokesperson under Hegseth and author of the new book " The President Deserves Better ."

Hegseth is seen as one of the chief Iran war backers in the administration — something Trump has publicly recognized.

"Pete, I think you were the first one to speak up, and you said let's do it because you can't let them have a nuclear weapon," Trump said in late March.

The pressure on Hegseth will go up next week as Massie, a vocal Iran war critic, plans to reintroduce eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, an effort that has House Democrats lining up behind it.

Massie, who lost his reelection to Hegseth-backed former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein, said the only thing that could stop him is Hegseth resigning on his own accord.

Mark Lucas, a Hegseth ally, said that Democrats are using Massie and Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) to drive the impeachment push and that his organization Veteran Action will hold any Republican accountable who supports the effort.

"And if you ever hope to have a political future in the Republican Party, you better vote that resolution down. It's bigger than Pete Hegseth. It's bigger than Donald Trump," Lucas said during his appearance on Steve Bannon's "War Room" show.

CBS News reported Wednesday that Trump was considering replacing Hegseth with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), who is term-limited and leaving office in January. However, one source said DeSantis is not interested in the role.

Trump has maintained that he has no plans to remove Hegseth from his role but noted in a phone interview with ABC News on Thursday that it would be easier to confirm a new Defense secretary while Republicans still have their majorities before next year.

The president also said Wednesday that Hegseth would be a "very popular" Tennessee senator if he filled Sen. Marsha Blackburn's (R) seat.

Hegseth is interested in the open Tennessee Senate seat , which expires in 2031, and has been campaigning behind the scenes for the post, The Hill previously reported . Blackburn has shown no signs of supporting the move.

"I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," the president told reporters Wednesday.

When pressed again on potential staffing changes involving Hegseth, the president said Thursday his Defense secretary "has done a fantastic job."

"We had more generals than we did in World War II. We had so many generals. Everybody was a four-star general. I never saw anything like it, and many of those people were woke," he continued. "I don't like a woke general, so he probably has opposition. I think he's doing a fantastic job."

Hegseth was seen walking into the West Wing earlier Thursday.

Massie also encouraged the president to replace Hegseth during the lame-duck period.

However, with only a few weeks of floor time and many competing priorities, replacing a defense secretary in the middle of a war may not be a top GOP priority.

Even if Trump did attempt a switch, a number of departing Republican senators who have locked horns with Trump, including Republican Sens. John Cornyn (Texas), Bill Cassidy (La.), and Mitch McConnell (Ky.), may not be generous with their confirmation votes.

On the Senate side, Democrats are quietly floating the defense secretary's removal following the midterms, using Hegseth as leverage in defense spending talks with the administration, The Hill previously reported . And they could have some GOP support.

Hegseth's message to service members on Thursday was to remain focused on the mission.

"To the troops, don't blink, ignore the noise, never hesitate," he said. "You see, all this is politics. You do real things, so stay the course."

articles.title: Hegseth expands National Guard operations in DC, authorizes police patrol cars, Humvees and boats
articles.summary: Pete Hegseth authorized 60 marked patrol cars, Humvees and D.C. National Guard boats as a council hearing demands the military presence be removed.
articles.body: War Secretary Pete Hegseth has authorized National Guard troops in Washington, D.C., to use dozens of marked police cars, military vehicles and boats as local officials demand an end to the deployment. Two Pentagon officials confirmed to Fox News Digital that Hegseth signed an Oct. 29 memo authorizing up to 60 marked patrol cars, Humvees, military tactical vehicles, D.C. National Guard boats and up to 20 light towers and generators. Roughly 3,000 National Guard troops are deployed in the nation's capital as part of President Donald Trump's crime crackdown. articles.title: Democrats won the midterms. That doesn’t mean voters like them
articles.summary: More than half of midterm voters said they had an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party, even as it won decisively.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Democrats won the 2026 midterms by a landslide, but that doesn't mean voters are happy with the party.

More than half of midterm voters — 52% — viewed the Democratic Party unfavorably, while 60% felt the same way about Republicans, according to NBC News exit polling .

Among those who backed Democratic candidates, roughly one in five had a negative view of the party as a whole, according to the AP Voter Poll .

The findings suggest Democrats have reason to be cautious after winning their biggest House majority since at least 2008 and flipping Senate seats in Republican strongholds like Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

"This was a repudiation of MAGA, not a vote for the Democrats," NewsNation's Chris Cuomo said Wednesday.

President Donald Trump had urged Americans to vote as if he were on the ballot, and many did, but not in the way he intended.

Just under half of voters — 44% — said opposing Trump was a reason for their House vote, versus just 16% who said it was to support him, according to NBC News.

Nearly two-thirds said Trump prioritizes his own interests over the country's, and a similar share blamed his policies for higher-than-usual prices.

"Midterm elections are primarily a referendum on the party in power," Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a progressive Maryland Democrat, told The Associated Press . "But we should be clear that that doesn't translate automatically into support for Democrats. We need to earn the support of voters."

Democrats have vowed to tackle the cost-of-living concerns that drove voters to the polls, but what that looks like remains to be seen.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren called for a "bold" agenda in a Thursday op-ed , urging Democrats to pursue economic populist policies that challenge corporate power and a "rigged system."

"Now it's time to act," Warren wrote. "Donald Trump says he wants to work with Democrats. We should force him to do that on the affordability and corruption issues that drove this election — or call his bluff."

Warren said Democrats should use the budget reconciliation process to "reverse Republican health care cuts, expand health care coverage and fund universal child care." She also pushed for a vote to ban stock trading by federal officials.

Sen. Bernie Sanders wants sweeping changes as well. He called on Democrats Thursday to pass "Medicare for All" when they take control of the Senate in January.

Other Democrats favor a more measured approach.

"I do not think it is time to propose things that the President of the United States is guaranteed to veto," Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii said in an interview before the midterms.

Schatz said Democrats need to win the White House and both chambers of Congress in 2028 to pursue a bolder agenda.

For now, he said, "I think people want to see us do, not everything, but a few things that will take the pain out of what they're experiencing."

Schumer faces questions about his plan to lead

Van Hollen told Bloomberg this week that Democrats should demand a "bold agenda" before backing Chuck Schumer or any other aspiring leader.

"No one should be committing to anybody as the next Democratic leader without having that conversation," Van Hollen said. "We need commitments."

Schumer expects to remain Senate Democratic leader, even though several incoming senators have said they won't vote for him, including Adam Hamilton in Kansas, Troy Jackson in Maine and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

"The issue is not me. I'll be reelected as majority leader. But the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want," Schumer said Wednesday when asked about the opposition within his own party.

El-Sayed said Thursday he would back Van Hollen for the role, but a source close to the Maryland senator told NewsNation that Van Hollen isn't running.

Schumer acknowledged Wednesday that Democrats still have work to do to win over voters.

"Many of the folks who voted for us yesterday, of course, are still skeptical. That's okay," Schumer said. "These voters did not give us the majority so we can do whatever we want. They entrusted us with the majority to do what they, the American people want."

articles.body:
Trump makes Oval Office a national monument

President Trump signed a proclamation Thursday seeking to designate two iconic White House spaces, the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, as national monuments.

Trump said Congress would have to ratify the proclamation , which would also make it so that no one could make “major modifications” to the rooms without congressional approval.

“It’s a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country,” Trump said of the Oval Office — where he announced the move to reporters.

“If anyone ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you call me, and I will come back here, and I will make sure it never happens,” the president added.

Trump has made a number of changes to the White House campus throughout his second administration, most notably knocking down the East Wing to build an up to $400 million ballroom without congressional authorization. Despite legal challenges to the project, the Supreme Court ultimately ruled construction could proceed .

A former Biden administration aide is projected to defeat Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., in one of the most closely watched races of the 2026 election cycle.

Cait Conley, a military veteran who served on the White House National Security Council, will likely be coming to Congress next year after beating the two-term incumbent for the job, The Associated Press projected late Thursday.

Multiple forecasts suggested the seat would be a likely pickup for Democrats.

Both parties poured enormous resources into the race for New York's 17th Congressional District in the months before Election Day. It was widely seen as key to both parties' quests to win the House majority.

The district, which sits just north of New York City, was won by Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

Lawler spent much of the race walking a political tightrope between supporting President Donald Trump and positioning himself as an independent voice.

And the race itself was marked by bitter divisions on issues like immigration enforcement and taxes.

Among Lawler's backers were the parents of Sheridan Gorman, a college student from his district who was killed in Chicago while she was out with friends. Gorman's accused killer is an illegal immigrant who was previously arrested for shoplifting, but was released without a federal immigration detainer because of Chicago's sanctuary city laws.

Lawler and Gorman's parents have pointed to her killing as proof that Democrat-backed sanctuary laws — which are active in New York as well — are deadly for Americans. He argued that Conley would do nothing to mitigate the effects of illegal immigration.

Conley, for her part, condemned Gorman's killing and has said she is against illegal immigration, but she has not spoken out against sanctuary laws specifically.

Conley served as counterterrorism director on the White House National Security Council from 2021 to 2023 and spent the remainder of former President Joe Biden's term as a senior advisor on election security at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

Fox News Power Rankings rated the district as "lean Democrat," while the Cook Political Report ranked it a toss-up.

articles.title: Ministério da Segurança: Lula faz reunião discutir recriação da pasta | G1
articles.standfirst: A criação de uma pasta específica para a área é uma promessa de Lula e foi reforçada pelo presidente após a aprovação da PEC da Segurança Pública pelo Senado.
articles.summary: O presidente Lula discute nesta sexta-feira a medida provisória para recriar o Ministério da Segurança Pública e fortalecer o combate ao crime organizado no país.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) faz uma reunião nesta sexta-feira (6) para discutir a recriação do Ministério da Segurança Pública.

A criação de uma pasta específica para a área é uma promessa de Lula e foi reforçada pelo presidente após a aprovação da Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) da Segurança Pública pelo Senado, na terça-feira (3) . O texto seguiu para promulgação.

Lula deve se reunir com os ministros da Justiça, Wellington César Lima e Silva, e com a ministra da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior, para discutir o tema e sobre uma medida provisória (MP) que deve ser enviada ao Congresso Nacional criando a pasta.

🔎 Medidas provisórias têm força de lei, mas precisam ser aprovadas pela Câmara dos Deputados e pelo Senado para se tornarem leis definitivas. O prazo inicial é de 60 dias, prorrogável por mais 60. A contagem é suspensa durante o recesso do Congresso.

Ao comemorar a aprovação da PEC, Lula afirmou que o novo ministério terá foco em inteligência, planejamento e cooperação com estados e municípios no enfrentamento a facções criminosas e milícias. Na ocasião, o presidente não informou quem comandará a pasta.

A PEC insere na Constituição o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (Susp) e amplia o papel da União na coordenação da segurança pública e no estabelecimento de diretrizes nacionais para o combate ao crime organizado . O governo ainda não informou quando o Ministério da Segurança Pública será recriado.

A nova pasta deverá ter papel na regulamentação e na implementação do novo sistema previsto pela PEC. Parte das mudanças dependerá de atos administrativos e parte, de projetos de lei que precisarão passar pelo Congresso.

Durante a campanha eleitoral de 2026, a criação do Ministério da Segurança Pública já constava no programa de governo de Lula .

A proposta previa que o órgão coordenasse, em conjunto com estados e municípios, políticas de combate ao crime organizado e promovesse maior integração entre as forças de segurança, com uso de inteligência e fortalecimento da Polícia Federal.

Presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). — Foto: Ricardo Stuckert

A ideia de um ministério exclusivo para a segurança pública não é inédita. A pasta foi criada em fevereiro de 2018 , durante o governo do então presidente Michel Temer (MDB), inicialmente por meio de uma medida provisória .

Meses depois, em julho, Temer sancionou a lei que tornou definitiva a criação do ministério.

O primeiro ministro da Segurança Pública foi Raul Jungmann, que deixou o Ministério da Defesa para assumir a nova estrutura.

Naquele desenho, passaram para o Ministério da Segurança Pública órgãos que até então estavam subordinados ao Ministério da Justiça, entre eles:

o Departamento Penitenciário Nacional (Depen);

a Secretaria Nacional de Segurança Pública (Senasp);

o Conselho Nacional de Segurança Pública;

e o Conselho Nacional de Política Criminal e Penitenciária.

Entre as atribuições estavam coordenar e promover a integração da segurança pública no país, em cooperação com estados, municípios e Distrito Federal, além de planejar e administrar a política penitenciária nacional .

A criação da pasta em 2018 ocorreu em meio à preocupação do governo federal com a crise na segurança pública. À época, o governo Temer afirmava que o ministério teria a função de integrar e coordenar as ações de segurança entre a União e os estados.

Em fevereiro daquele ano, Temer assinou um decreto de intervenção federal na segurança pública no estado do Rio de Janeiro . Com isso, o governo assumiu o comando da segurança pública do estado, com a prerrogativa, inclusive de reestruturar as instituições e demitir e contratar pessoa para atuarem na segurança

Em 2019, ao assumir a presidência, Jair Bolsonaro optou por reunir novamente Justiça e Segurança em uma única pasta , chefiada pelo ministro Sérgio Moro. O ex-presidente chegou a considerar recriar a pasta, mas proposta não foi adiante.

A discussão sobre a recriação do ministério ocorre logo após a aprovação da PEC da Segurança Pública pelo Senado . O texto foi aprovado em dois turnos na terça.

Entre outros pontos, a proposta incorpora o Susp à Constituição e prevê maior cooperação entre União, estados e municípios. Também estabelece medidas voltadas ao combate a crimes violentos, facções criminosas, organizações paramilitares e milícias.

O Susp já havia sido criado por lei em 2018 e prevê uma atuação coordenada entre os governos federal, estaduais e municipais na área de segurança.

O Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública defendeu a recriação imediata do ministério após a aprovação da PEC. Segundo a entidade, uma pasta autônoma poderia coordenar a implementação do Susp e estabelecer protocolos de cooperação e de intercâmbio de informações entre órgãos públicos.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed's pattern of hostile exchanges with reporters draws scrutiny after viral moment
articles.summary: Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., went viral for putting his hands on Sky News reporter James Matthews in a tense Election Day exchange.
articles.body: Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., went viral this week for his latest altercation with a reporter, putting a spotlight on a history of tense exchanges with the press. El-Sayed had a combative exchange with Sky News reporter James Matthews just hours before his victory in Tuesday's midterm elections. The exchange began when the British journalist attempted to question El-Sayed, but it was hardly the first time El-Sayed appeared to either lose his temper, interrupt a journalist or respond sharply to a reporter. Heritage Foundation media fellow Tim Young is well aware that President Donald Trump also has a long history of criticizing reporters, but he believes the situations are "completely different." "El-Sayed gets angry at the media for asking actual questions about him and his relationship to organizations like the Muslim Brotherhood. He legitimately doesn’t want to answer those questions, so he snaps," Young told Fox News Digital. ABDUL EL-SAYED PUTS HANDS ON SKY NEWS REPORTER IN HOSTILE CONFRONTATION HOURS BEFORE ELECTION VICTORY "Trump gets asked the same narrative-shaping questions all the time, then watches networks create false narratives about him on air, which makes him angry," Young continued. "The two are not the same." El-Sayed recently scolded a reporter for asking him about Democratic Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens, sarcastically declaring, "You’re really asking the questions that the people want to hear." "Ask me a serious question," he added. El-Sayed also got testy with NBC News anchor Tom Llamas in October after Llamas questioned him about allegations involving his family's ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. "It’s funny to me. I was born in 1984, down the street in Rochester Hills. I was raised here in Michigan, went to the University of Michigan, rebuilt the health department in this city, led the health department in this county, and you want to ask me about Egypt in 1970? Are you serious?" he retorted. El-Sayed then accused Llamas of using "hearsay evidence from a tweet" and suggested the "NBC Nightly News" anchor was "not serious" before asking, "Are you insinuating that somehow I was lying?" EL-SAYED MOCKS TRUMP, VANCE AND ROGERS IN GLOATING VICTORY SPEECH SIGNALING COMBATIVE TONE IN SENATE That same month, El-Sayed shut down Free Press reporter Audrey Fahlberg for asking about private comments he made on leaked audio regarding some Michigan residents mourning the death of Ayatollah Khamenei. El-Sayed insisted he would answer questions about gas prices and groceries but declined to "talk about leaked audio" and accused Fahlberg of seeking clickbait. "I’m just not interested in this dog and pony show," El-Sayed said. "Ask smart questions." Fahlberg responded that his thoughts on Khamenei were relevant considering he frequently discusses foreign policy, but El-Sayed refused to engage. Fahlberg later said El-Sayed appeared to become furious whenever asked about the Iranian regime. Weeks later, El-Sayed clashed with Fox News "Special Report" anchor Bret Baier, repeatedly interrupting Baier during an exchange over the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed has also spoken about confronting media personalities. "You know how many terrible things Bill Maher has said about people like me? Terrible, awful things," El-Sayed said during a September interview with Chuck Todd. "I would go on that show," El-Sayed continued. "I wanna give people the image of watching him get his a-- whooped on his own show by a guy who prays like I do." UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN STUDENTS RALLY BEHIND ABDUL EL-SAYED AFTER HIS SENATE WIN OVER MIKE ROGERS As for El-Sayed’s latest encounter, the viral Election Day moment occurred when he walked up to Matthews and asked, "Are you registered to vote in the state of Michigan?" "I'm not," the British U.S.-based correspondent responded. "Why would I care to have a conversation with you?" the Democrat fired back. After Matthews answered that he was a journalist, El-Sayed scoffed while responding, "In the U.K." "You know how many votes I want to get in the U.K.? Zero," El-Sayed told Mathews as he put both his hands on the reporter's shoulders. "I'm never running for office in the U.K." Matthews stressed that the 2026 U.S. midterm election "matters to the world" and told El-Sayed he was "bidding to be a senator." "A senator in where? What country? What country?" El-Sayed replied while placing his hands on Matthews' shoulders again. "The United States," Matthews answered. "What country are you with?" El-Sayed then asked. "I'm based in the United States," Matthews said. "But you report for where? Where are your viewers?" El-Sayed interrupted. El-Sayed dismissed Matthews after the reporter explained that Sky News serves an international audience, insisting "Sky News is not viewed in the United States of America," then sneering that "like five people" watch the network in the U.S. "I've answered all the questions. I've answered all the questions for the viewers of the United Kingdom. So, I'm going to ask you to stop chasing me around. Please," El-Sayed said before walking away. Matthews denied to El-Sayed he was "chasing" him around. "If you keep being in my way, I'm not going to be very happy," El-Sayed told the reporter. EL-SAYED MOCKS TRUMP, VANCE AND ROGERS IN GLOATING VICTORY SPEECH SIGNALING COMBATIVE TONE IN SENATE Footage of the incident quickly went viral, and many observers criticized El-Sayed for physically touching the reporter. Piers Morgan called it "pathetic" and "very patronizing." Reason’s Reem Ibrahim said El-Sayed "looks like an absolute p---k" and former Israeli spokesperson Eylon Levy called him a "bully." Students for Trump founder Ryan Fournier called the behavior "unhinged," while Spencer Pratt asked, "Why is this angry little Elf Sayed so comfortable putting hands on another man like that?" Communications trainer Jocelin Martinez, who provides media training and message development to clients, doesn’t feel El-Sayed needs to change his approach after he crushed Republican rival Mike Rogers in the critical Senate race for a seat Republicans were hoping to flip this election cycle. "El-Sayed's communication style got him elected in Michigan because the moment requires leadership with gumption," Martinez told Fox News Digital. The El-Sayed campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital’s Joseph A. Wulfsohn contributed to this report.

articles.title: Failed GOP redistricting in South Carolina, Indiana would have backfired: DDHQ
articles.summary: Republicans across the country redrew congressional maps for their benefit ahead of the 2026 midterms, but it failed to yield them gains in most places. An analysis shared Thursday shows it could have been worse. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana rejected efforts to implement GOP-friendly maps that could eliminate all Democratic seats, which…
articles.body:
Republicans across the country redrew congressional maps for their benefit ahead of the 2026 midterms, but it failed to yield them gains in most places. An analysis shared Thursday shows it could have been worse.

Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana rejected efforts to implement GOP-friendly maps that could eliminate all Democratic seats, which Democrats at the time took as a win in their fight to retake the House majority.

But a new analysis from nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s polling partner, shows that if these maps had passed, they likely would have backfired badly for the GOP and led to even larger gains for Democrats.

Applying House votes in South Carolina to the proposed redraw, Democrats would have won three of the state’s seven congressional districts — despite the map intending to elect Republicans to all of them, DDHQ’s analysis found. Democratic candidates won two seats on the current map.

Palmetto State Democrats showed surprising strength Tuesday night as Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Sen. Darline Graham (R). Andrews would have carried five districts under the proposed map, according to DDHQ.

In Indiana, applying the results from the statewide election for secretary of State, Democrats would have carried all nine of the redrawn districts — also designed for a GOP sweep. Democrats in Indiana ultimately won three districts on the current map.

The Indiana secretary of State’s race was unusually high-profile this year, as Beau Bayh (D), son of former Sen. Evan Bayh (D) and grandson of former Sen. Birch Bayh (D), won the race by 9 points.

The redistricting proposals were the center of controversy in Republican politics after a few GOP state senators in Indiana blocked the map changes President Trump pushed for. In response, Trump backed primary challengers to the senators who voted against the map, and many of the incumbents lost.

In South Carolina, Republicans considered drawing out Rep. James Clyburn (D) but ultimately decided against it , despite pressure from the president.

Many states did end up redistricting ahead of the midterms, including Florida, Texas, North Carolina and Tennessee. Maps in those states did not deliver the gains they expected, DDHQ found.

Florida Republicans tried to flip four Democratic seats with a redraw and got zero. And while aiming to draw five new seats for the GOP, Texas Republicans won just one additional seat and lost two others.

North Carolina Republicans pushed maps to try and oust Rep. Don Davis (D) in the 1st Congressional District. Davis held on, and the GOP came within a couple points of losing every congressional seat in the Tar Heel State.

Ohio Republicans’ new map should have drawn out two Democratic incumbents, but both held on, and Democrats flipped three other seats in the Buckeye State.

And in Tennessee, while Republicans did narrowly flip the seat they targeted, the GOP incumbent in the 4th Congressional District is trailing with nearly all votes counted — a seat Trump won by 24 points in 2024 that was not thought to be a Democratic target.

articles.title: Child molester's looming prison release reignites sanctuary showdown in wake of Dem election sweep
articles.summary: DHS warns convicted child molester Leomar Zambrano could be released in Seattle as sanctuary city officials refuse to honor the ICE detainer.
articles.body: A convicted child molester and illegal alien from Venezuela could soon be back on the streets unless authorities in Seattle ditch their sanctuary city policies and cooperate with federal immigration enforcement. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has sent a detainer request to the liberal Pacific Northwest enclave for Leomar Alexander Lopez Zambrano, asking that he be turned over rather than be released back into the U.S. after his prison sentence concludes. The clash between DHS and Seattle exacerbates longstanding tensions between President Donald Trump’s immigration officials and leaders in so-called sanctuary cities, which have thrown up roadblocks to law enforcement cooperating with federal enforcement authorities. Going a step further, the outcome of Tuesday's elections are putting even more of a microscope on the agency at the center of much controversy during Trump's second term and is raising questions about which administration officials could face the wrath of a brand-new blue Congress. DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN "Sanctuary politicians in Washington are refusing to honor the ICE detainer and hand this disgusting criminal over to us after he finishes his prison sentence," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement. "This illegal alien has been convicted on TWO counts of child molestation." After the 2026 midterms, the matter in Seattle raises new questions of whether sanctuary cities will feel emboldened to double down on their efforts to block Trump's agenda as Democrats prepare to retake a majority in the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives. To those like Hans von Spakovsky, an immigration expert with Advancing American Freedom (AAF), the political tide turning in Washington, D.C., might encourage Democrat-run cities to go even further in stonewalling immigration enforcement agencies and making it harder for officials to do their jobs. "I have no doubt that sanctuary jurisdictions will feel emboldened," Spakovsky told Fox News Digital in the days after the Republican bloodbath. "I also would not put it past [Democrats] to try to impeach Tom Homan for imagined wrongs because he has been the most effective czar of immigration enforcement of any administration in the past 50 years," he said. "I don’t think they would be successful, but, again, that will embolden defiance of federal immigration enforcement in sanctuary jurisdictions." In many cases, sanctuary cities simply cut off communication with federal law enforcement, and DHS fears that will be the case with Zambrano, the convicted Venezuelan child molester. Zambrano is now approaching the end of a 15-month sentence, the point at which he would normally face deportation. But Mullin noted DHS would have no way of knowing when he was out of jail without Seattle's cooperation. articles.body:
Republican Amanda McKinney, a Yakima County commissioner, is projected to win the race for Washington’s 4th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ.

McKinney defeated Air Force veteran John Duresky (D) in the battle for the seat, which covers a large portion of the eastern half of the Evergreen State. Eastern Washington is more rural and tends to lean more Republican than the bluer western half of the state on the other side of the Cascades.

The race between McKinney and Duresky had been rated as solidly Republican by the nonpartisan political handicapper Cook Political Report.

McKinney has previously worked as a mortgage banker and a small-business owner. Beyond her campaign for Washington’s 4th District, she has done political advocacy on issues like vaccine mandates, agriculture and opposing Cascades grizzly bear reintroduction.

The representative-elect, who locked down endorsements from President Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), will succeed retiring Rep. Dan Newhouse (R-Wash.) in his seat. Newhouse was one of the Republicans who voted to impeach Trump following the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot.

“A very successful Business Executive, Civic Leader, and Highly Respected Yakima County Commissioner, Amanda has dedicated her life to serving her Community,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in January.

articles.title: Meet the unexpected winners of this year’s midterms
articles.summary: While Democratic victories in marquee national contests took the spotlight this week, with the party securing at least 250 seats in the House and winning bac...
articles.body:
While Democratic victories in marquee national contests took the spotlight this week, with the party securing at least 250 seats in the House and winning back the Senate, several candidates in down-ballot races across the country clinched what appear to be surprising wins.

Gen-Z college students win in Arizona, Georgia and Massachusetts

Nineteen-year-old Sebastian Matta will likely be the next Superior Court clerk of Maricopa County, Arizona, as he is leading his Republican opponent Jeff Dial, a former state lawmaker, by more than 85,000 votes as of Thursday evening, according to the county's unofficial results .

Matta, an Arizona State University student, would oversee an office that maintains records for the court that handles criminal and civil cases in Arizona's most populous county.

"I saw that nobody on the Democratic side had submitted themselves to this office in nearly a decade," Matta told The Arizona Republic. "And I figured, 'You know, why not?'"

He told the outlet he never expected to win, but said he was "very overwhelmed with happiness" when he realized he had been a substantial lead over Dial. He's has vowed to make the court more accessible, particularly for those that speak languages other than English.

Dial told the newspaper he had called Matta to concede.

In Georgia, 22-year-old Benjamin Culberson defeated his Republican opponent in a race for a seat on the Gwinnett County Commission by more than 10 percentage points, according to the state's unofficial results . According to CNN affiliate WSB-TV , the Georgia Gwinnett College student flipped the seat, and the commission will now be made up of all Democrats.

19-year-old Daniel Darris-O'Connor , a student at the University of Massachusetts Lowell, unseated longtime incumbent Republican Marc Lombardo to win a seat in the Massachusetts House of Representatives. He'll be one of the youngest lawmakers in state history.

He acknowledged his age in an interview with CNN-affiliate WCBV , insisting that his campaign was focused more on the issues than the fact that he was a young person running for office. He recalled how the Covid-19 pandemic, which began when he was in middle school, was an "eye opener that the world isn't perfect and we need new leaders in our government that are actually going to fix things."

A candidate who had suspended his campaign wins in Iowa

Eric Armstrong, who suspended his campaign in September for an Iowa state House seat currently held by Sen.-elect Josh Turek citing health issues, is expected to win the race anyway as he is ahead of Republican Keith Jones by around 10 percentage points, according to the state's unofficial results Thursday evening.

In a social media post on Thursday, Armstrong announced that he would take office at the beginning of next year. "The voters of District 20 sent a clear message about the direction they want for Iowa, and I will make sure that message is carried to the Capitol in January," he wrote.

"Thank you to every voter who placed their confidence in this campaign. I will continue to do my best and be open and upfront about what comes next," he added.

Texas couple Marcus and Sheree Henderson will be the only two Democrats leadership positions in Kaufman County, which is in the northeastern part of the Lone Star State, according to county election results .

Marcus Henderson will serve as Justice of the Peace, while Shree Henderson will sit on the Kaufman County Commissioners Court, a panel that votes on tax rates and oversees the county's budget. A local news outlet reports that they are the first Democrats to be elected to the county in this century.

A GOP stronghold in New Jersey elected its first Democrat in more than 50 years

Unofficial results show that pharmaceutical representative Christopher Russo won his race for county commissioner in Morris County, a Republican stronghold in New Jersey, by over 20,000 votes, becoming the first Democrat elected to a countywide office there since 1973, according to the New Jersey Globe .

CNN's Steve Contorno and Jeff Simon contributed to this report.

articles.title: Surprise twist ricochets through Supreme Court case on AR-15 ban
articles.summary: A blockbuster Supreme Court appeal challenging a ban on AR-15-style semi-automatic rifles may be thrown into disarray by a mysterious request to remove the l...
articles.body:
A blockbuster Supreme Court appeal challenging a ban on AR-15-style semi-automatic rifles may be thrown into disarray by a mysterious request to remove the lead plaintiff from the case, a puzzling twist that prompted the ban's defenders to ask the justices on Thursday to dismiss the case.

The case, which the Supreme Court has scheduled for argument next month, centers on a Cook County, Illinois, ordinance that makes it unlawful to sell or possess any "assault weapon or large capacity magazine," including AR-15 rifles.

Two Illinois men claimed the ban violates the Second Amendment. But in a one-paragraph filing last week, attorneys for the lead plaintiff, Cutberto Viramontes, asked to be removed from the litigation without explanation.

Thursday, Cook County said that if Viramontes is removed, it would make the case moot — meaning that the justices would throw it out.

"Viramontes has not offered any explanation as to why he sought to remove himself from the suit," the Cook County State's Attorney, Eileen O'Neill Burke, a Democrat, told the Supreme Court in the filing. "And the most natural inference from the barebones motion is that Viramontes' circumstances have changed in some significant fashion."

Viramontes' attorneys at the Cooper & Kirk law firm have not responded to CNN's repeated requests for information about why he wants to leave the case.

On one level, whether Viramontes is permitted to withdraw would have limited practical significance for the broad question of whether state and local governments may ban AR-15-style rifles.

The Supreme Court simultaneously granted a second case in June, challenging Connecticut's similar ban, which would continue even if the Supreme Court decided to dismiss the Cook County litigation. And whatever the court decides on Connecticut's ban would almost certainly affect whether other bans like the one in Cook County can stand.

On the other hand, Viramontes' unexplained departure raises questions about the vetting law firms conduct when they file suits on behalf of plaintiffs that, from the start, are intended to move the law by setting a nationwide precedent.

The other individual plaintiff in the case, Christopher Khaya, doesn't intend to purchase an AR-15 but rather a weapon called an IMI Galil, another semi-automatic rifle that is similar to an AK-47. While there's no question that the gun Khaya would like to purchase is also banned by Cook County, the Supreme Court focused the question it will answer in the case on the AR-15 and "similar semiautomatic rifles."

Gun rights groups, meanwhile, have leaned heavily in their written arguments on the ubiquitousness of the AR-15, not on the type of weapon Khaya is seeking.

"There are no record facts concerning whether the IMI Galil weapon operates similarly to an AR-15," Cook County argued in its Thursday filing. "There are also no record facts concerning whether the IMI Galil weapon is 'in common use for lawful purposes,' which petitioners maintain is central to the Second Amendment inquiry."

CNN has reached out to the attorneys for Viramontes and Khaya, as well as two Second Amendment advocacy groups in the case, for reaction to the Cook County motion. One of those groups, the Second Amendment Foundation, noted that the Supreme Court will almost certainly rule on the underlying issues regardless of what happens with Viramontes.

"There is every reason that this case should continue, both on behalf of the remaining individual plaintiff, as well as on behalf of SAF's members," the group said in a statement that also noted the Connecticut case. "This issue will be addressed by the Supreme Court."

A similar dynamic unfolded last year when a transgender woman challenging Idaho's ban on trans athletes told the Supreme Court that she wanted to withdraw her case because of intense "negative public scrutiny" and a desire to focus on "academic and personal goals." The attempt by the student athlete, Lindsay Hecox, underscored the difficulty advocacy groups have experienced in sustaining legal challenges given the attention significant major culture war cases receive at the Supreme Court today.

The high court deferred Hecox's request and then, in June, ultimately ruled against her . The transgender sports dispute also involved two cases, including one that dealt with a high school student in West Virginia.

In addition to the Second Amendment Foundation, a group called the Firearms Policy Coalition is also part of the Cook County suit. But to establish their right to sue, known as standing, associations generally need to identify at least one member who would have standing to sue on their own.

The appeals over AR-15 rifles are among several Second Amendment matters that have reached the court following its massive 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, which struck down a strict requirement in New York that residents show cause to obtain a carry permit.

As part of that decision, a 6-3 conservative majority said that in order to survive Second Amendment scrutiny, modern-day gun regulations need to have some grounding in the "nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation."

Cook County and Connecticut have argued there is a long historical tradition of the government regulating weapons that are "unusually dangerous," and they argue that AR-15s fall squarely in that category. The county opened one of its briefs with a list of mass shootings that involved "assault weapons," and the number of people killed in those incidents. "2022 Highland Park parade , 7 dead; 2022 Buffalo supermarket , 10 dead," it read. The list continued for more than three pages.

Connecticut expanded an earlier ban in 2013 in response to the mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School months earlier.

But gun rights groups have focused more on a 2008 precedent in which the Supreme Court held that citizens have a right under the Second Amendment to possess a weapon "in common use." The groups challenging the bans say that an estimated 20 to 30 million AR-15-style rifles are in circulation and they have described the AR-15 as "the most popular rifle in the country."

Ten states have enacted similar bans on AR-style rifles.

This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.title: Vance ‘privately’ blasts Netanyahu as Iran war divides Trump administration and 2028 ambitions loom
articles.summary: JD Vance privately accused Benjamin Netanyahu of being "wrong on everything" about the Iran war as he positions himself for a 2028 presidential bid.
articles.body: Vice President JD Vance privately accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of being "wrong on everything" about the Iran war, according to reports, as disagreements over the conflict expose tensions within the Trump administration and raise questions about Vance's potential 2028 presidential ambitions. The clash, reported by Axios Nov. 4., comes after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections and Vance publicly blamed the war for the party's defeat while urging President Donald Trump to pursue a negotiated settlement rather than renewed military strikes. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote later on Wednesday on X. VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY' "Low-level hostility between Vance and Netanyahu is beneficial for Vance," Natan Sachs, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, told Fox News Digital. "It allows him to give some distance from the Trump administration, which has just taken a huge electoral beating, but also to position himself ... in a very different position than President Trump himself without attacking Trump." Vance has also led a faction of senior administration officials urging Trump to negotiate an end to the conflict, warning that the unpopular war could cost Republicans control of Congress, according to reports. Netanyahu had urged Trump to resume strikes against Iran ahead of the midterms, but Trump held off after endorsing Netanyahu for re-election in Israel. Sachs said Vance's main concern appeared to be the prospect of overthrowing Iran’s government after Netanyahu presented Trump with a plan for regime change. "Many opposition leaders in Israel, nonetheless, are very skeptical of the idea that you can bring about regime change through an air campaign," Sachs said, adding that such a campaign could have the opposite effect. "You may strengthen the regime." As previously reported by Fox News Digital, Vance had also declined to endorse Netanyahu’s re-election campaign and criticized Israeli government officials who opposed Trump's efforts to end the Iran war. The Israeli election further complicated the relationship, Sachs said, leaving Netanyahu's political future uncertain and raising the possibility that Vance could have to work with a different Israeli leader. NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE "If Netanyahu is not the leader of Israel, Vance will find himself with another decision to make. Does he continue with a line that is confrontational with a new Israeli leadership, or does he say, 'Well, it was all Netanyahu; now we can see a different path forward'?" Sachs said. "Netanyahu is a very easy target here, both because there are very real differences of opinion, and Netanyahu's role was important, but also because this way he can criticize the war, criticize Netanyahu, and not say any bad word about Trump." Roughly six in 10 voters said U.S. military action against Iran was the wrong decision, according to the AP Voter Poll. "I think what's remarkable here is that it's coming out now," Sachs said. "And it's part of the fact that about midnight Wednesday, the next presidential campaign in the United States began, and JD Vance is trying to position himself. "He is breaking with the policy of President Trump, although he's doing so by criticizing Netanyahu, never Trump." VANCE REVEALS THE TRUMP DILEMMA THAT COULD COMPLICATE HIS 2028 WHITE HOUSE AMBITIONS Nonetheless, Vance has played a leading role in efforts to end the conflict with Iran, including direct outreach to senior Iranian officials. Last month, he sent a letter through Qatari intermediaries to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, proposing renewed peace negotiations. According to Axios, the letter said any negotiations to prevent further U.S. military strikes must address Iran's nuclear program. A U.S. official said Trump backed the outreach. Rezaei later confirmed receiving the letter but said he had not responded. "My suspicion is that JD Vance was operating on behalf of Trump on this," Sachs claimed. "Trump, after the war sort of settled after the first few weeks, appointed Vice President Vance to try and negotiate the exit strategy, and Vance has been very keen on that." Sachs also cited Vance's involvement in an earlier memorandum of understanding with Iran as further evidence of his preference for diplomacy. "He agreed to the MOU, which has become quite notorious in the United States, giving quite a bit to the Iranians, much more than the administration is now considering reasonable. VANCE TAKES LEAD SELLING TRUMP’S IRAN GAMBLE AS RUBIO, HEGSETH AND RATCLIFFE CEDE SPOTLIGHT ON FRAGILE DEAL "Vance has certainly been on the side that has been trying to achieve a diplomatic breakthrough." The White House is now weighing whether to resume major strikes against Iran, maintain economic and naval pressure or pursue a negotiated settlement. On Thursday, Reuters reported that Tehran submitted a formal nuclear proposal to the United States through Qatari intermediaries, making further negotiations contingent on Washington addressing its seven demands. "The real question is whether the Americans and the Iranians can approach some kind of agreement on the fundamentals, starting with freedom of navigation in the Straits of Hormuz and the cessation of hostilities," Sachs said. For Vance, the dispute poses a political balancing act of distancing himself from a war he reportedly opposed while serving as vice president in the administration that launched it. articles.title: Trump signs order to prevent future presidents from changing Oval Office
articles.summary: The order comes after Trump made a series of big changes to the decor of the Oval Office and tore down the White House East Wing.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office.

Trump, a former real estate mogul, has drastically altered the look of the president's official office during his second term, most notably with adding many gold features.

"We're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday.

The order comes months after Trump tore down the entirety of the White House East Wing in a project that has faced legal challenges.

The project was also approved by the US Congress. Construction has continued, with plans to turn the space into a new ballroom.

American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress.

The executive order, which Trump signed on Thursday, declares the Oval Office to be a national monument, along with some of its surrounding rooms.

The document also says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character".

"We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country," Trump said, adding that world leaders who have visited in recent months have complimented his decorative changes to the room.

Trump said the White House and the Oval Office had been in need of repairs before his changes, calling it "badly damaged". He described broken windows, cracked walls and broken stone.

Many of the noticeable changes, though, were cosmetic, including a large gold plaque reading "Oval Office" outside the space, paving over the Rose Garden and adding a new helicopter pad.

Trump said the order would "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space".

The entire building is already designated as a National Historic Landmark, which is intended to prevent against sudden changes to the building.

As president, Trump has the power to create national monuments, which are similar to national parks.

Trump's order calls on the office to be maintained by the National Park Service "in a manner that protects its historic character, architectural integrity, and association with the Presidency".

It notes the existing protections to the White House, but says "nonetheless, the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance".

Congress has carved out an exemption to the National Historic Preservation Act, in order to allow presidents to make needed changes. The current Oval Office has existed since the early 1930s, after its conception by President Franklin D Roosevelt.

Greg Werkheiser, from the law firm Cultural Heritage Partners, which specialises in historic preservation, says that temporary alterations like "furniture and decor is completely up to the president's discretion".

"As long as they're not damaging the permanent art and architecture, they can generally do whatever they want," he told the BBC.

Werkheiser argues that the Trump administration has shown disregard for other historic sites in Washington and, through lawsuits, has attempted to undermine the laws that require preservation.

Trump has undertaken a massive beautification project in Washington and has held three events in the past week to boast of the construction, even as his Republican party was trounced by Democrats in the midterm elections.

Werkheiser called Trump's order "hypocrisy", noting the various projects he's pushed for across Washington - including plans to build a new triumphal arch, which has been temporarily put on hold by a federal judge , and renovating the Kennedy Center.

"On the one hand he's talking about the importance of preserving the Oval Office - which is legally meaningless because he can't do it - and on the other hand he is absolutely taking an axe to the law that allows us to preserve other historic sites."

In October, the president suggested in an interview with Time magazine that the Oval Office would need to be torn down due to security concerns from the US Secret Service.

"I said, 'My ass, you can't build a new one. This is a special place,'" Trump said at the time.

During the midterm election campaign, Democrats criticised Trump's redesigns, with former President Barack Obama saying that his golden tweaks have "got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory".
