articles.title: White House denies Hegseth, Rubio will leave jobs amid Republican election fallout
articles.summary: US media reports there are calls to replace Pete Hegseth, who also faces a possible impeachment vote, while Mark Rubio is rumoured to be eyeing a presidential run.
articles.body:
The White House has denied rumours that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio might leave their jobs in a post-election shakeup of the Trump administration.

US media have reported there are calls to replace Hegseth - in particular over his handling of the Iran war, which is being blamed for heavy Republican election losses.

One outgoing congressional Republican has threatened to force an impeachment vote against Hegseth as early as next week. The defence secretary posted a video statement defending his record and denouncing the effort.

"You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."

Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war

Meanwhile, Rubio is denying reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.

Working for Trump until the end of his term has "always been my plan," Rubio told The New York Times in an interview.

"I love the work I'm doing," Rubio said. "And plus I always laugh when they say he's going to leave his job. I go, 'Which one?'"

The White House and US State Department also shut down reports that Rubio might be leaving after this week's midterm losses, with both calling it "fake news".

The defence secretary, though, faces a more uncertain political future.

Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have both blamed the Iran war for Republican losses that allowed Democrats full control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

In a telephone interview with ABC News, Trump said that he had received "calls about" Hegseth, but added that he had "every intention" of keeping him.

Later on Thursday, he told reporters at the White House that "Pete Hegseth has done a fantastic job", and went on to list what he sees are some of his achievements, including the arrest of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in January and the Iran war, now into its ninth month.

The Washington Post reported on Thursday that Trump might be, however, considering ousting General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Centcom chief Admiral Brad Cooper. Both played significant roles in offering guidance on the war, which started eight months ago.

Meanwhile, Republican Representative Thomas Massie, a frequent critic of Trump, has said he will push ahead with plans to push for Hegseth's impeachment.

He told news site Politico that he will trigger his resolution to impeach the defence secretary early next week.

And on X, he warned that the president should replace Hegseth before a new Democratic-controlled Congress forms in January.

"He should do it while he can still get the replacements confirmed in the Senate," Massie wrote on X.

Hegseth has also been rumoured to be interested in running for an open Tennessee Senate seat.

In his video statement, Hegseth denounced the "sham articles of impeachment" effort against him from a "disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies", and listed ways the department has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda under his leadership.

That includes, he said, reviving military recruitment, rebuilding the defence industrial base, and rooting out diversity initiatives.

Of the Democrats, he said: "Their policies don't work. So their obsession with political theatre disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It's all about the politics of personal destruction."

articles.title: Trump focuses on White House decor for second straight day in post-midterm remarks
articles.summary: The president signed a proclamation that he said would prevent major changes to the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room by future presidents without congressional approval.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is using his postelection public appearances to talk about the lasting physical changes he hopes to leave behind at the White House. In the two days since Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections, Trump has spoken twice in public. Both times he focused on rooms and renovations at the White House. On Thursday, Trump signed a proclamation that designates the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room as a national monument in an effort to block any significant changes to them by future presidents. “We’re going to be declaring it a national monument, and we’re going to send it over to Congress to have it ratified,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “It won’t be able to be taken down, destroyed, touched or anything else.” Trump, who later took questions from reporters about other topics, said any “major modifications” to the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room would have to be approved by Congress, adding that he hopes “the people in Congress will be smart enough not to let that happen.” The White House has officially been a U.S. National Historic Landmark since 1960. Trump wrote in the proclamation that “the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance.” The signing ceremony came a day after Trump spoke to reporters at the construction site for the new White House ballroom he’s building. Even though it was his first time addressing the media publicly after the Democrats swept several seats in deep red states to secure control of Congress, he focused his comments on the ballroom. “I’m doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America and it’s got to be pristine — it’s got to be perfect,” Trump said, adding that he felt “it would be appropriate to have the media here.” Unlike the ballroom project, which involved demolishing the historic East Wing and has attracted criticism from preservation groups, the Oval Office often undergoes cosmetic changes with each new administration. When Trump returned to office last year, he completely redecorated the Oval Office, filling it with his signature favorite: lots and lots of gold. The proclamation signed Thursday states that future presidents would still be able to “redecorate” the Oval Office and “select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications,” as long as they don’t “substantially impair the monument’s historic structure or architectural character.” In discussing the proclamation, Trump also emphasized the “victories” he has achieved in the Oval Office, though he added, “I mean, there’s been some mistakes, too.” He didn’t elaborate. Asked what he hopes Congress will focus on while Republicans still hold the majority for the next two months, Trump brought it back to himself. “It’s been a tremendous two years. I don’t think there’s ever been a president that’s done more,” he said, speaking of his efforts at the border and on the stock market. Trump’s final campaign message, on Monday, also centered in large part on his renovation efforts. That speech was held at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, which has been closed since July because of “botched” renovations made after Trump requested upgrades. He spent the majority of Monday’s remarks touting the pool’s reopening and his other renovation efforts around Washington.

In discussing the proclamation, Trump also emphasized the "victories" he has achieved in the Oval Office, though he added, "I mean, there's been some mistakes, too." He didn't elaborate.

Asked what he hopes Congress will focus on while Republicans still hold the majority for the next two months, Trump brought it back to himself.

"It's been a tremendous two years. I don't think there's ever been a president that's done more," he said, speaking of his efforts at the border and on the stock market.

Trump's final campaign message, on Monday, also centered in large part on his renovation efforts.

That speech was held at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool , which has been closed since July because of "botched" renovations made after Trump requested upgrades. He spent the majority of Monday's remarks touting the pool's reopening and his other renovation efforts around Washington.

articles.title: Democrat Jessica Killin flips longtime GOP-held Colorado House seat
articles.summary: Democrat Jessica Killin is projected to unseat Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colo.) in Colorado’s 5th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Killin’s win marks a political first for the Colorado Springs-area district, which has never elected a Democrat since its creation in 1973. The Army veteran, who previously served as chief of staff to…
articles.body:
Democrat Jessica Killin is projected to unseat Rep. Jeff Crank (R-Colo.) in Colorado’s 5th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Killin’s win marks a political first for the Colorado Springs-area district, which has never elected a Democrat since its creation in 1973.

The Army veteran, who previously served as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff, capitalized on growing voter frustrations over rising gas prices tied to the ongoing Iran war and President Trump’s economic agenda .

Her victory also underscores the shifting political landscape in a district Trump carried by roughly 9 percentage points in 2024, giving Democrats a significant pickup in their bid to regain control of the House.

The race grew increasingly competitive in the final stretch of the midterm cycle. The Cook Political Report shifted the contest from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican” in September, while DDHQ’s preelection forecast still projected a roughly 7-point GOP margin.

Killin centered her campaign on affordability, healthcare and military families, while also criticizing the Trump administration’s decision to relocate the U.S. Space Command headquarters from Colorado Springs to Alabama.

Crank, a former conservative radio host and Americans for Prosperity executive, was first elected in 2024 following the retirement of longtime Rep. Doug Lamborn (R-Colo.).

During his first term, Crank largely supported Trump’s legislative agenda, including the GOP’s “ One Big Beautiful Bill Act .”

articles.title: 2 House Democrats float idea of Blanche impeachment
articles.summary: Two House Democrats are already floating the impeachment of Attorney General Todd Blanche after the GOP’s sweeping midterm election defeats, suggesting Democrats could win enough Republican support in the Senate to remove him from office. Reps. Hank Johnson (D-Ga.) and Deborah Ross (D-N.C.) voiced their support for impeaching Blanche on Thursday, just two days after…
articles.body:
Two House Democrats are already floating the impeachment of Attorney General Todd Blanche after the GOP’s sweeping midterm election defeats, suggesting Democrats could win enough Republican support in the Senate to remove him from office.

Reps. Hank Johnson (D-Ga.) and Deborah Ross (D-N.C.) voiced their support for impeaching Blanche on Thursday, just two days after Democrats won control of both the House and Senate.

“I personally believe that the offenses of Todd Blanche demand that he be impeached and convicted and removed from office,” Johnson said in an interview with SiriusXM’s “The Dan Abrams Show.”

“That’s my personal opinion. I think his efforts to undermine the rule of law can’t go unaddressed,” he added.

Johnson was responding to a question from host Dan Abrams about how Democrats could address the Department of Justice (DOJ) alleged use of its authority to pursue political retribution under President Trump.

Ross, who appeared on the program after Johnson, agreed with Johnson’s assessment, but also suggested Democrats target Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth first.

“100 percent,” Ross said when asked whether she supported impeaching Blanche. “But I think we should start with Hegseth.”

The Pentagon chief could face an impeachment vote as soon as next week, with Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) spearheading the effort.

Ross said she also expected an impeachment resolution against Blanche, telling Abrams, “I can’t imagine we won’t have one.”

She pointed to Democrats’ newly won Senate majority as a reason impeachment proceedings could have a different outcome than previous efforts to remove Trump from office.

“When you’ve got 56 Democrats, and there are still some Republicans who have bucked Trump who are there, there is a chance that some of this will happen,” Ross said.

Blanche’s leadership at the DOJ has faced renewed scrutiny, including its intervention in Alaska’s Senate election.

Trump directed the department to file a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the race under certain circumstances if Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) lost to Democrat Mary Peltola, arguing that the addition of a candidate with a similar name to Sullivan’s could confuse voters and potentially affect the outcome of the race.

The DOJ also saw a high-profile departure on Thursday when Harmeet Dhillon, the head of its Civil Rights Division, announced her resignation following months of criticism over her handling of civil rights enforcement.

articles.title: Washington voters approve transgender athlete ban
articles.summary: Washington voters are projected to reverse the state’s long-standing policy that has allowed transgender girls to compete on girls’ and women’s school sports teams, according to Decision Desk HQ. The ballot measure will require students to submit documentation from a healthcare provider verifying their sex before playing on a girls’ team. It’s a major loss…
articles.body:
Washington voters are projected to reverse the state’s long-standing policy that has allowed transgender girls to compete on girls’ and women’s school sports teams, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The ballot measure will require students to submit documentation from a healthcare provider verifying their sex before playing on a girls’ team.

It’s a major loss for transgender rights advocates in the blue state. Washington joins 27 states across the country that enacted similar laws prior to Tuesday’s elections, according to the Movement Advancement Project .

But those efforts began in Republican-led legislatures, while this year’s push in Washington came from voters in a state that tends to lean Democratic. Similar measures are on the ballot Tuesday in Arizona, Colorado and Nebraska.

Washington’s Initiative 638, also known as the Defending Equity in Interscholastic Sports Act, requires school districts and nonprofits to “prohibit biologically male students from competing with and against female students” when a sport has a gender divide.

Existing state law requires athletes to undergo a physical exam. Now, the provider during the exam must verify the student’s sex if they want to play on a girls’ team. Providers are instructed to rely on “reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels.”

Earlier this year, the Supreme Court rejected arguments that transgender athlete bans violate Title IX or the Constitution’s equal protection guarantee in a 6-3 vote along ideological lines .

In recent weeks, Washington’s existing policy has brought the issue back to the high court.

A mother whose daughter says a transgender girl sexually assaulted her during a wrestling match wants an exemption from having to compete against a transgender girl in the future. Lower courts rejected the argument, but she filed an emergency appeal with the justices.

It has been ripe for a decision for nearly three weeks, but the justices have yet to act, letting Election Day come and go in the meantime.

images.caption: Signs are held by demonstrators against transgenders in sports are seen outside the Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, January 13, 2026 as court hears oral arguments in the Little v. Hecox and West Virginia v. B.P.J. regarding transgender rights in women’s sports.

articles.title: Hinojosa vows to protect Texas citizens from data centers
articles.summary: Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) vowed to protect Texans from data center projects after she is sworn into office in January. “Well, we have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans,” Hinojosa said during an appearance on…
articles.body:
Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) vowed to protect Texans from data center projects after she is sworn into office in January.

“Well, we have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans,” Hinojosa said during an appearance on CNN on Thursday night. “And right now, what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans, and Texans are being taken advantage of.”

She plans to implement “laws to protect Texans” and to stop working with data centers “until we have those protections.”

“We can have a strong economy, strong industry, and protections for the people of Texas. Those things are not mutually exclusive, and I’ll make sure, as governor, I lead to ensure that that happens,” she expressed.

CNN’s Jake Tapper clarified that Hinojosa is not ruling out data centers being built in the Lone Star State, but that the incoming governor wanted “there to be regulations to protect communities. Is that right?”

“And that communities have a seat at the table to decide if and how these data centers come into their communities. Texas is like a country. We are so diverse in all ways,” Hinojosa responded. “So, absolutely, we need to make sure they are partners in this effort, and that has always been my position. It is not that I hate data centers. I hate the way they are taking advantage of Texas, and that stops when I’m governor.”

Hinojosa’s defeat of outgoing Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) happened alongside Democratic wins down the ticket . Abbott conceded and told supporters that he would “assist her and her team in a period of transition.”

While on the campaign trail, Hinojosa took the populist approach toward data centers, tuning into voters’ sentiment about the ultrawealthy who may own the facilities.

She previously vowed to establish a moratorium on data center construction throwing existing data center build-out in Texas into uncertainty.

Worry about Hinojosa’s positions has caused Texas state Rep. Brian Harrison (R) to call on Abbott to curb her power before next year. He warned in a social media post that Hinojosa should not have “unchecked emergency powers,” and that “the urgency is undeniable… and inaction is intolerable.”

articles.title: NCPC approves plan to build Trump’s triumphal arch
articles.summary: The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) on Thursday voted to approve plans to build a triumphal arch championed by President Trump between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. The motion to approve the project passed by an 8-4 vote after listening to over 100 public remarks largely against the project after a nearly 9-hour…
articles.body:
The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) on Thursday voted to approve plans to build a triumphal arch championed by President Trump between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The motion to approve the project passed by an 8-4 vote after listening to over 100 public remarks largely against the project after a nearly 9-hour meeting .

The commission approved the project during a virtual meeting that crashed at around 2:30 p.m. EST during public testimony before resuming roughly 40 minutes later. The stream moved to the NCPC’s YouTube channel after the stream crashed on its official government website.

NCPC Vice Chairman Stuart Levenbach reminded those listening that the commission’s “role is to evaluate the purpose from the standpoint of…the design of the project,” adding that the proposed Arch would transform a “tired traffic circle” into a “monumental gateway.”

The arch will be located on Columbia Plaza on the Arlington Memorial Bridge, symbolically linking Washington, D.C., and Virginia as a sign of unity following the national division that led to the Civil War in the 1860s.

Public testimony challenged the commission to not approve the plan, with many arguing that it was an insult to the service members and their relatives buried at Arlington and claimed that it was a vanity project spear-headed by Trump.

Many discussed the arch’s impact on D.C.’s airspace endangered those in the area, with one speaker referencing the 2025 midair collision over the Potomac River that killed 67 people.

Several even called in from the protest site on the Memorial Bridge with their background showing the proposed arch with a red “X” covering it.

Former CIA analyst Holly Fletcher slammed the commission for how history will view them ahead of the vote. She called the arch “pointless” and “tasteless,” asking if commissioners want to side with “this mad king,” referring to Trump.

“Honestly, listening to your mental acrobatics and inexplicable sycophancy today, I am already embarrassed for you,” she said before the vote. “Because mark my words, Trump and his movement will not succeed … And we will remember your names and what you choose to do in this moment.”

“Do you want to be complicit in shameful, autocratic lunacy, or do you want to join our historic movement for democracy?” she added.

Ed Sterling, Vice President of Government Affairs for the National Parks Conservation Association, asked the commission why it could “give final approval to a structure that doesn’t even have a clear purpose?”

Sterling noted that studies under Section 106 of National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) had also been “cut short.”

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) was the first to comment against the arch, saying that “revered presidents” were honored with structures in Washington after they served. He added, after emphasizing the lack of congressional approval on the project, that the U.S. is a “nation of laws, not kings or kangaroo commissions.”

NCPC chair Mark Paoletta challenged Huffman’s remarks, telling the California Democrat that he was “wrong” about the 1925 congressional authorization for the Arlington Memorial Bridge Commission, which the Trump administration has cited as its reasoning to construct the arch a century later. He said he was “wrong” in indicating that that project was “just about a bridge.”

Huffman replied that citing this and other historical records differed from congressional authorization or “legislative history.” He said he didn’t think that information will “fly” amid the court battle over the arch, “but you should try that argument in court and let’s see where it goes.”

At least two Republican House members spoke out in favor of the arch, Reps. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.) and Brian Mast (R-Fla.).

images.caption: FILE – President Donald Trump holds up a model of the proposed triumphal arch as he addresses a dinner for donors who have contributed to build the new ballroom at the White House, Oct. 15, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/John McDonnell, File)

articles.title: Judge blocks construction of Donald Trump's massive arch
articles.summary: The Trump administration had hoped the building of the 250-foot arch could begin as early as this week.
articles.body:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in Washington.

US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.

Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch.

Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people.

The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the US president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.

The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment.

It is not yet clear when construction of the arch could start, as a number of lawsuits are seeking to block it.

A rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.

The Trump administration has said the arch would double as a complex to store military equipment - complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.

"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump previously wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch". He did not specify to which cities he was referring.

Mark Paoletta, the chairman of the NCPC and one of the Trump appointees, said at Thursday's meeting that the president understood "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments".

He and other commissioners said the structure fulfils a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island, just as Congress and various commissions intended.

Paoletta added that the arch would honour the nation, its veterans and "provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves".

Anne Wright, who spent 29 years in the US military and also worked in the diplomatic service, told the BBC she would try to stop the construction.

"We'll tie ourselves to the bulldozer, we've got veterans in wheelchairs and we'll chain the wheelchairs to these things," she said.

Wright referenced this week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress, saying: "[Trump's] policy of war, of ego – they've been rejected."

Fellow veteran John Pomeroy - who served in the Air Force for six years, including during the Vietnam War, and whose parents are buried at Arlington - said the arch "would lessen the solemn nature of a visit to the cemetery".

He described Trump's suggestion that the arch could store military equipment as "silly" and a "half-baked idea", arguing it would be a target for terrorist attacks.

Like Wright, Pomeroy said he would "impede construction workers as much as I can" if they came to the site to begin work.

Trump signs order preventing future presidents from changing Oval Office

Democratic Congressman Jared Huffman argued in his statement to the commission that the arch would disrupt sightlines not just of Arlington but of the Lincoln Memorial, fracturing "a view meant to underscore the unity and sacrifice of the American people, and doing that with a structure we often associate with emperors or kings who built grand arches as tributes to themselves".

"This is a tribute to Donald Trump," Huffman added.

Lawsuits have been filed against the plans, raising concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety. There is also a disagreement over whether congressional approval is needed to build the arch.

It is one of several construction projects Trump has proposed for the US capital. That includes at the White House, where he is facing legal challenges over the construction of a ballroom, which is estimated to cost $400m (£300m).

His plans to renovate a 106-year-old golf course, which he has dubbed "trash island", is also being challenged in the courts.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth strikes defiant tone in face of impeachment threat
articles.summary: Many lawmakers, including some Republicans, have criticized the defense secretary over his handling of the Iran war.
articles.body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday dismissed a renewed effort in the House to bring articles of impeachment against him as early as next week. In a video on social media, Hegseth said, “A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice.” Hegseth was referring to Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who said Wednesday that he plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment when the House is back in session. Lawmakers are scheduled to return to Washington on Monday. “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth added. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.” In the more-than-five-minute video, Hegseth only briefly touched on the Iran war — a driving force behind the effort to impeach him, as well as GOP losses in this week’s midterm elections. Massie, who lost his GOP primary after he crossed Trump, urged Trump on Thursday to replace Hegseth while he still has a GOP majority in the Senate. “My Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress. They’ll have hearings & trials,” he said on X. “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns,” Massie wrote Wednesday. Numerous Democrats have indicated a desire to oust Hegseth since their midterm election wins, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to be the next speaker. Trump said Wednesday that he is not planning to replace Hegseth, and he said Thursday that Hegseth “has done a fantastic job” and “probably has opposition” over the actions he has taken, including purging military leadership. Trump has told some allies he is considering replacing Hegseth, asking them who they think should succeed him, two people familiar with discussions told NBC News this week. He has previously insisted that he was not considering dismissing department heads just days before they were shown the door. Massie tried to force a vote on impeaching Hegseth in September, but his efforts were stunted when House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., sent the House home early. He would need several Republicans to join all Democrats in supporting the impeachment measure for it to succeed. The House has impeached only two Cabinet officials in history — former President Joe Biden’s homeland security secretary, Alejandro Mayorkas, in a partisan vote, and William Belknap, the secretary of war in the 1870s. No Cabinet members have ever been convicted by the Senate.

images.caption: Pete Hegseth, US secretary of defense, during a news conference at the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, US, on Wednesday, April 8, 2026.

articles.title: Trump issues proclamation declaring Oval Office national monument
articles.summary: Following election losses, the signing marks Trump’s third event of the week focused on signature renovation projects.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has signed a proclamation designating the Oval Office and the adjacent Cabinet Room as a national monument.

Signed from behind the president’s desk, topped with a red “VETO” baseball cap, the proclamation on Thursday marked Trump’s first official action since his party’s sweeping losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections , which will hand Democrats control of Congress come January.

“We’re making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office at the signing, adding that the document will turn both rooms, located on the first floor of the West Wing, into “a landmark for the ages”.

The monument also includes the Outer Oval Office. The move is intended to prevent any major changes to the spaces, which the president has heavily redesigned during his second term in office.

The effort is also aimed at preserving the spaces’ “historic character, architectural integrity, and association with the Presidency”, according to the proclamation.

The proclamation orders the interior secretary to manage the monument through the National Park Service, and requires “documentation, review, and consideration of alternatives before any action that would substantially alter or demolish the monument”.

The measure does not prevent future presidents from restyling the Oval Office. Proclamations can be revised or revoked by a successor via a new executive action – a strategy Trump himself used to dramatically downsize two major national monuments in Utah during his first term, and again during his second term after former President Joe Biden had fully restored them.

The text of the proclamation also explicitly states that the order does not restrict the president’s authority to redecorate, select furnishings or change the office’s decor.

Coming on the heels of his party’s defeat , the signing marked the president’s third event of the week highlighting his pet projects.

Those initiatives include multiple high-profile overhauls, including the demolition of the East Wing to build a highly contentious , nearly $1bn White House ballroom to sit atop a multistorey underground bunker, as well as a proposed 76-metre (250ft) triumphal arch along the approach to Arlington National Cemetery.

These projects, including the failed renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, which cost more than $14m, have drawn sharp criticism from opposition lawmakers and many Americans. Public opinion polls have signalled that many voters are dissatisfied with the Trump administration’s domestic spending choices and broader economic priorities.

Inside Trump’s multimillion-dollar White House renovations

Since returning to office in 2025, Trump, a real estate mogul-turned-politician, has started numerous construction projects and added personalised flourishes throughout the White House.

In June last year, Trump installed two towering flagpoles on the North and South Lawns, and later paved over the Rose Garden’s lawn with a stone patio reminiscent of his luxurious Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida.

The South Lawn is also home to a newly installed multimillion-dollar granite helicopter pad, intended to protect the lawn from damage by the new presidential helicopters.

Inside the White House, the president has given the Oval Office a golden makeover, with gleaming vases, 24-karat gold trim on the ceilings, burnished wood carvings, and heavy gilded frames spilling across multiple surfaces.

In September last year, Trump lined the West Wing Colonnade with an exhibition of presidential portraits, dubbed the “Presidential Walk of Fame”. The display features controversial plaques with gold lettering beneath the portraits, which include partisan criticisms of some former presidents, including Barack Obama.

Trump did not elaborate on precisely what he was hoping to prevent but suggested that the Oval Office might face some threat in the future.

The president’s administration has faced several lawsuits alleging that his Washington beautification projects were carried out without the necessary approval.

“If anybody ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you call me wherever I may be,” Trump said, “and I’ll come back here and I’ll make sure it never happens.”

images.caption: US President Donald Trump holds a signed proclamation establishing the Oval Office National Monument in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, DC, on November 5, 2026 [Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters]

articles.title: Federal judge temporarily blocks construction of Trump's Arlington triumphal arch hours after approval
articles.summary: The National Capital Planning Commission had approved construction for President Trump's proposed triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., hours before the restraining order was issued.
articles.body: A federal judge early Friday temporarily blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., just hours after a federal planning commission approved the project. articles.title: Data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
articles.summary: (AP) — After a campaign season filled with outrage against data centers, the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the e...
articles.body:
HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — After a campaign season filled with outrage against data centers , the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

A tougher regulatory environment for artificial intelligence giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if President Donald Trump — perhaps the industry's biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown.

Data center regulation itself was not on most midterm ballots, and it wasn't among the top issues for most voters. But hardline stances against the server warehouses were woven into the platforms of many candidates, including the Democrats who upended longtime Republican control of the governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa, many of which are data center hotspots.

Skepticism of data centers, and their impact on electricity prices , often blended with the fight for affordability — a key campaign talking point for Democrats.

In Texas, Clayton Tucker, the first Democrat elected state agriculture commissioner since 1986, said his pledge to fight data center development was critical to his victory. Everywhere he went, he said, ranchers worried that data centers posed an existential threat to their dwindling water supplies.

"You know, there's an old saying around here that 'whiskey's for drinking and water's for fighting,'" Tucker told The Associated Press. "And that's exactly what happened."

Data centers were a persistent bogeyman in attack ads

According to data from AdImpact, campaigns large and small spent more than $380 million on television ads mentioning data centers. Democrats outspent Republicans on the topic by more than three to one.

Sweeping wins by Democrats could have far-reaching implications for data centers. Besides taking control of Congress, Democrats flipped at least five governors' offices and took full control of state governments in five more states: Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Michigan.

Data Center Watch, a project of AI security consultancy 10a Labs, said it tracked winning candidates for Congress and governorships and found the vast majority had expressed support for stronger regulation or even a moratorium.

Among governors, 32 of the 34 victorious candidates in races where AP called a winner support stronger regulation or restrictions. Twelve of the 34 support bans or moratoriums, it said.

During the campaign, Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley, a Democrat, changed his position under pressure from his Republican opponent to take a harder line against data centers. Initially opposed to any moratorium, Crowley later said he supported one as well as abolishing the state's sales tax exemption for data center operators and developers.

In an interview Thursday with AP, Crowley said he's having discussions now about what he'll propose once he takes office.

In the mix are things like requiring developers to disclose more about their water and energy consumption, ensuring a community supports a project before it can go forward and insulating ratepayers and taxpayers from the energy costs of the projects, Crowley said.

AI giant OpenAI published a framework Thursday enumerating new commitments to the communities where it develops data centers. The company said it was asking federal, state and local policymakers to write "clear rules for how the industry builds."

"Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared," the post said.

An industry association, the Data Center Coalition, echoed the sentiment that developers need to keep trying to build trust with public officials and communities. A coalition official, Dan Diorio, said the industry is aware many midterm winners have vowed to impose a moratorium.

"We should expect them to want to deliver on those promises, but there are going to be real world consequences of that," Diorio said in an interview.

Those consequences, Diorio said, could include host communities missing out on tax revenue or payments from tech companies. Data centers are also driving a broader economic expansion that encourages investment in domestic manufacturing, he said.

Wall Street sees red lights ahead after the election

The election of data center skeptics adds challenges to stock markets riding high on the AI boom .

On Thursday, the Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11% below its all-time high amid worries that data center construction may slow because it's getting costlier to borrow money .

AI data center construction is driving much of the U.S. economy's growth , and any slowdown could have a broader chill.

In an analyst report, Morgan Stanley said decisive results for Democrats carry "greater expectations for data center restrictions" that, under new state regulations, could "split the country into areas that are open to new data centers and those without."

It singled out Texas' election of Democrat Gina Hinojosa for governor as the "most important election result" for data center development. Hinojosa has said she'd block a permit for a data center if it wasn't a good deal for Texans or residents hadn't gotten a say in the matter. She defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who had touted Texas as "the epicenter of AI development" before trying to clamp down on it late in the campaign.

Morgan Stanley also said Ohio's election of Democrat Dr. Amy Acton as governor "creates significant risk of data center project delays in the state." Acton has pledged to block a data center project unless it meets certain standards.

Local elections didn't go well for data centers, either

Voters in local referendums cast ballots overwhelmingly in favor of restricting data centers, according to an analysis by polling and data science firm Redbud Consulting.

Redbud tracked 47 referendums in 44 municipalities in 12 states, including 21 in Ohio alone, eight in Maine, seven in Illinois and four in Kansas. Restrictions were approved in 44 of the 45 elections where counting was complete, Redbud reported.

Most voters don't want a data center built near them

About three-quarters of U.S. voters oppose the construction of a new data center in their community, according to The AP Voter Poll.

In red and blue states alike, majorities of voters were opposed to adding a data center where they live.

Support was higher in some traditionally red states, including Wyoming, West Virginia, Louisiana and Mississippi. In Texas, voters in the Senate race were similarly likely to say they oppose a new data center being built in their community.

Despite voters' deep opposition to data centers near them, The AP Voter Poll suggests it was not a particularly motivating issue in this election.

About one-quarter of U.S. voters said AI data centers were "crucial" to their vote for Congress, which is well below the shares that said government corruption or the cost of living were highly important to their vote.

The stakes were especially high in Texas

Texas is poised to overtake northern Virginia as the largest global data center market by 2030, according to a report by commercial real estate giant JLL.

In the campaign, Hinojosa aggressively attacked Abbott as having rolled out the welcome mat for data centers.

Stephen Sanders, a Republican who co-founded a data center protest group in Lubbock, said Texans were especially attuned to the issue because of talk that data centers pose a threat to their electricity and water in the drought-stricken state.

"I would say data centers were on the ballot," Sanders said.

Associated Press reporters Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles and Linley Sanders in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title: Judge blocks construction on Trump's 250-foot arch for now
articles.summary: The National Capital Planning Commission voted Thursday to approve plans for President Trump's 250-foot triumphal arch. A judge quickly blocked any construct...
articles.body:
Washington — A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from beginning construction on President Trump's proposed triumphal arch late Thursday, siding — for now — with a group of Vietnam veterans and the District of Columbia and Virginia, which sued to stop the project.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that the government cannot start any "construction-related activity" for 14 days, while further legal proceedings play out. In a 33-page ruling , Chutkan wrote that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in showing the federal government did not follow required legal processes before moving to build the 250-foot triumphal arch. She also said Virginia and D.C. likely have standing to sue, pointing to "tangible economic harms" caused by traffic problems at the construction site.

The ruling came shortly after the National Capital Planning Commission voted Thursday night to approve plans for the arch, giving the final go-ahead for the monument that's set to be constructed between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The NCPC, which acts as the federal government's planning agency for the region and is stacked with Trump allies, voted 8-4 to greenlight the project after almost 9 hours of public comments from members of Congress, veterans, architects and Washington, D.C., and Virginia residents.

Chutkan's order aside, it's unclear how soon construction of the arch could start, though the Justice Department said in a court filing last month that it could begin as soon as Thursday.

In a separate filing Wednesday night, the Trump administration said that a construction company "may be — but is not necessarily — arranging off-site preparations for construction mobilization in anticipation of permit approval" at the site.

Ahead of the meeting, the NCPC's executive director, Mark Paoletta, recommended approval of the final site and building plans for the structure, which is supposed to celebrate 250 years of American independence.

Paoletta, the top lawyer at the Office of Management and Budget, heralded Mr. Trump's "historic vision" for the structure and said it would be the "grandest arch ever built by mankind."

But California Rep. Jared Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, said during the hearing that the arch is "illegal" and would "disrupt the solemn connection" between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

"This arch would dishonor America, our ideals, and our laws," Huffman said during remarks to the planning commission, adding that Congress is the appropriate body for debating the proposed monument.

One Marine veteran who spoke in opposition to the proposal, Jimi Shaughnessy, said "a dominating arch with a carnival-like atmosphere of tourists, food trucks and buses is abhorrent and insulting to those who gave all and to their families."

"Instead of focusing on the issues facing military families, this administration is intent on spending taxpayer dollars to site, plan, and design a monument no one asked for, and are content with bypassing any laws or regulations that may prevent them from breaking ground," he said.

The arch itself will be 166 feet tall and topped with "three gilded figures" — a gold, winged female figure flanked by a gold flying eagle on each side — bringing its overall height to 250 feet, according to documents filed with the NCPC. The structure will sit close to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, though the Federal Aviation Administration determined it will pose "no hazard to air navigation," with a "condition for safety lighting that includes a non-standard eternal flame and continuous floodlighting."

The arch will also feature an observation deck, and the Trump administration has estimated that it could draw between 2,000 and 22,400 visitors each day.

It's expected to take three years to build the arch, which will be located in the center of what is called Memorial Circle, across the Potomac from the Lincoln Memorial. It's unclear how much the project will cost, and who will foot the bill.

Mr. Trump said in September that his "Triumphal Arch" would be a "top grade Military Complex" and house drones and sniper ammunition. But the documents from the NCPC do not include the military usage.

Lawyers for the Justice Department declined to provide more details about the national security features in an October hearing.

The commission received more than 1,300 public comments about the project, most of which were in opposition, it said.

The NCPC's approval comes as Chutkan weighs how to act. A group of Vietnam War veterans, as well as the Commonwealth of Virginia and the city of Washington, D.C., have filed lawsuits arguing that the Trump administration is acting without congressional authorization and is not complying with the required procedures to construct the monument.

In an order Tuesday, Chutkan required the government to provide her notice within one hour of any NCPC vote and a thirty-minute notice to any preparation for construction of the arch to give her time to issue a decision on whether to block construction.

The government filed the required notices late Thursday, and Chutkan responded by issuing a temporary restraining order that blocked "construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at the site.

In a hearing last month, Chutkan said the most important issue for her is whether the Vietnam War veterans had the legal right to sue. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court found that a group of plaintiffs who brought a similar suit to block the White House ballroom construction likely did not have legal standing to challenge the project.

In court filings, the Justice Department called the plaintiffs' motions "breathless" and urged Chutkan to follow the Supreme Court's decision in the White House ballroom case, but attorneys for the groups of plaintiffs argued that their legal arguments were different than the ballroom case and urged Chutkan to halt the arch's construction.

Two of the plaintiffs, Vietnam veterans Michael Lemmon and Shaun Byrnes, told Chutkan in a hearing last month that the arch construction would impact their experience when visiting graves at Arlington National Cemetery, and said they would be harmed by the arch's size and purpose.

In a separate suit brought in late October, Virginia and the District of Columbia sued, and the case was assigned to Chutkan, who had heard arguments the day before from the Vietnam veterans group. The state's attorneys general argued that "as soon as Defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm" on them because "the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges."

articles.title: Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results?
articles.summary: BBC Verify examines whether US voters were influenced by the data centre boom - and the impact anti-AI sentiment could have on the industry.
articles.body:
A US midterms voter poll has suggested data centres were a highly motivating issue for many Americans, leading some to argue public backlash against the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure construction boom might have helped shape the election outcome.

BBC Verify has looked at its role in the campaign and examined the potential consequences for the AI industry.

The poll for AP and a consortium of news organisations found 56% of surveyed voters said data centres were a "crucial or major" factor in their vote, while 76% said they would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community.

The hostile sentiment was considerably stronger among those who said they voted Democrat at this election.

This follows other recent Pew Research polling which suggested about half of Americans think data centres are "mostly bad" for the environment, home energy costs and quality of life, a big deterioration in favourability since January.

The congressional voter poll results certainly suggest a remarkable degree of salience for a subject which likely would not have been on most Americans' radar five years ago.

However, it is some way behind several key issues people considered "crucial or major factors" in their vote, including government corruption (90%) and the cost of living (89%).

Did the AI backlash affect Senate races?

Three of the Senate seats flipped by the Democrats have significantly more data centres , Texas (595), Ohio (258) and Iowa (117), than the median of 55 across all 50 states.

And Texas alone has 31 ongoing data centre construction projects, the most of any state .

But other factors would also have been motivating voters in these states, as elsewhere.

BBC Verify analysis of state-level voter polling for Senate elections suggests states which swung to the Democrats either followed the national trend over data centre concerns, or seemed less concerned.

So we can't say how many votes or Senate seats were directly delivered by data centre opposition.

But it's notable that three key states in the US AI build-out, Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all elected Democrats as senators and governors who called for tighter regulation on data centres in one form or another.

requirements to fully cover their own energy and water infrastructure costs

mandates to use unionised construction workers

stricter environmental and transparency safeguards

What could the election results mean for the future of the AI boom?

The US economy has been heavily supported in recent years by massive corporate investments in AI , including for data centre construction.

Official data shows inflation-adjusted monthly spending on building data centres, excluding the IT hardware to go into them, in August 2026 was $5bn (£4.2bn) - five times higher than in 2023.

Analysis by Columbia Business School suggests AI infrastructure investment in the US is currently larger as a share of the overall economy than spending on new railways was at the height of that boom in the 19th Century.

Cori Crider, executive director of the Future of Tech Institute, a European think tank, told BBC Verify the industry should anticipate that new state leaders will put conditions on or "even stop runaway data centre build".

Seema Shah, from global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said requirements for developers to pay for additional investment in the electricity grid, meet tougher standards over their usage of resources like water, or give up tax incentives could "raise development costs and slow new supply".

However, Heather West from the Eurasia Group consultancy said temporary bans on construction and new regulations might delay the data centre roll out, but would not stop it entirely.

She said "projects already permitted or under construction will largely proceed", but delays would affect the "next wave" of building through "local fights, slower permitting, and pressure to make data centres pay for their own power".

Analysts from the consultancy Oxford Economics have said there are also strong economic incentives for politicians to avoid policies that would severely disrupt data centre construction, pointing to tax revenue and construction jobs they bring.

Deepak Surana of the Futurum Group, a technology research firm, said he expected there would ultimately be "a negotiation, not a moratorium" from Texas state leaders on data centres to ensure no negative impact on residents' energy and water bills.

OpenAI, which has a data centre in Texas and under-construction projects in Ohio, pledged to ensure it fully paid for its own electricity on Thursday - one day after the midterm results.

Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett
